---
title: "correlation & statistical tests"
---

## why check this before modelling

- [checking each feature's distribution](feature-engineering.qmd#check-the-distribution-before-transforming) looks at one column at a time; this step looks at relationships — between features, and between each feature and the target — before committing to a model
- it catches redundant features, flags assumed relationships worth questioning, and gives a cheap first pass at which features are worth keeping before spending compute on a full model

## correlation between features

- **pearson's r**: measures linear association, $r=\dfrac{\operatorname{cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}$, ranges from $-1$ to $1$ — assumes a roughly linear relationship between two continuous variables and is sensitive to outliers
- **spearman's rho**: rank-based; measures monotonic (not necessarily linear) association, and works for ordinal data — more robust to outliers than pearson
- **kendall's tau**: also rank-based, generally more robust with small samples or many tied ranks than spearman, at higher computational cost
- a correlation matrix (often as a heatmap) is the standard way to scan pairwise correlations across many features at once
- highly correlated feature pairs (roughly $\lvert r\rvert>0.8$–$0.9$, context-dependent) carry mostly redundant information — consider dropping one, combining them, or leaning on [regularisation](regularisation.qmd) (ridge in particular) rather than removing anything by hand

## multicollinearity: variance inflation factor

- the variance inflation factor (vif) quantifies multicollinearity for one feature by regressing it on every other feature: $\text{vif}_j=\dfrac{1}{1-r_j^2}$, where $r_j^2$ is the $r^2$ from that regression
- a vif above roughly 5–10 is commonly flagged as problematic multicollinearity
- multicollinearity mainly destabilises coefficient estimates and their interpretation in linear/logistic regression — it usually hurts predictive accuracy far less than it hurts interpretability, see [covariance matrix](../foundations/covariance-matrix.qmd) for why near-singular $x^\top x$ causes this

## correlation & association with the target

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| target type | feature type | typical check |
|---|---|---|
| continuous | continuous | pearson or spearman correlation |
| continuous | categorical | anova f-test (does the continuous variable's mean differ across categories) |
| categorical | continuous | anova f-test (same idea, roles reversed), or compare the feature's distribution per class |
| categorical | categorical | chi-square test of independence |
| either | either | mutual information — captures any dependency, not just linear or monotonic, at the cost of not saying direction or size |

:::

## statistical tests cheat sheet

::: {.table-responsive tabindex="0"}

| test | compares | typical use | key assumption |
|---|---|---|---|
| pearson's r (+ its t-test) | linear correlation between two continuous variables | is a correlation significantly different from 0 | roughly linear relationship, roughly normal residuals for the significance test |
| spearman's rho | monotonic correlation, can be ordinal | pearson doesn't fit — nonlinear or ranked data | monotonic relationship |
| independent t-test | means of a continuous variable between 2 groups | e.g. is a biomarker's average different between treatment and control | normality within each group (or large $n$), roughly equal variances |
| welch's t-test | same as above | same as t-test, but group variances differ | normality (or large $n$), no equal-variance assumption |
| mann-whitney u | distributions of a continuous/ordinal variable between 2 groups | non-parametric alternative to the t-test when normality doesn't hold | independence only, no normality needed |
| anova (f-test) | means of a continuous variable across 3+ groups | comparing a feature's mean across multiple target categories | normality, roughly equal variances across groups |
| kruskal-wallis | distributions across 3+ groups | non-parametric alternative to anova | no normality assumption |
| chi-square test of independence | association between two categorical variables | is there a relationship between two categorical features, or a feature and a categorical target | expected cell counts not too small (rule of thumb $\geq5$) |
| shapiro-wilk | whether a sample looks normally distributed | checking the normality assumption before choosing a parametric test | sensitive to sample size — large samples often reject even trivial deviations |
| kolmogorov-smirnov | a sample against a reference distribution, or two samples against each other | similar role to shapiro-wilk; also used to compare train/test feature distributions | continuous data |
| levene's test | equal variance across groups | checking the equal-variance assumption before anova or a standard t-test | — |

:::

- read a p-value as: how surprising this data would be if the null hypothesis were exactly true — not as the probability the null hypothesis is true
- statistical significance and predictive usefulness are related but distinct: a significant test doesn't guarantee a feature helps a model, and a non-significant one doesn't guarantee it's useless — validate with a model and cross-validation, not a p-value alone, see [train/test splits](train-test.qmd#cross-validation)
- testing many features at once inflates the chance of a false positive by chance alone (the multiple comparisons problem) — correct with methods like bonferroni or benjamini-hochberg (fdr control) when screening many features

## practical considerations

- choose parametric tests (t-test, anova, pearson) when normality roughly holds and sample size isn't tiny; otherwise prefer the non-parametric alternatives (mann-whitney, kruskal-wallis, spearman) — check normality first with shapiro-wilk or a qq-plot, see [check the distribution before transforming](feature-engineering.qmd#check-the-distribution-before-transforming)
- compute correlations and run tests using the training fold only, to avoid leaking target information into feature selection — see [avoiding leakage](feature-engineering.qmd#avoiding-leakage)
- these are fast, cheap pre-screens, not a full feature-selection pipeline — they look at one feature at a time and miss interactions a model might still pick up; pair with the wrapper/embedded methods in [feature selection & extraction](feature-engineering.qmd#feature-selection-extraction) rather than relying on tests alone
